name: Days a penny a day apart
brief:
`prices[i]` is a share's closing price in pence on day `i`. A pair of days `i < j` is steady when the price rose by exactly one penny for each day between them, so `prices[j] - prices[i] == j - i`. Return the number of steady pairs.

Write `count_steady_pairs(prices)`.

Example. For `[5, 6, 4, 8, 9]` days 0, 1, 3 and 4 are each steady with the others, which makes 6 pairs. Day 2 is steady with none. The answer is 6.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ days, each price a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Checking every pair of days is too slow.
All tests share a 5-second time limit. Answers can pass $10^{10}$.
hint: Move the days to one side: the condition says `prices[i] - i` equals `prices[j] - j`. Count how often each value of `prices[i] - i` has been seen.

examples.note: The values of price minus day are 5, 5, 2, 5, 5, and four equal values make 6 pairs.
Price minus day gives 10, 7, 10, 7, 10. Three 10s make 3 pairs and two 7s make 1, so 4.

how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Rewriting the condition as `prices[i] - i == prices[j] - j` turns it into counting equal keys.
Steady days need not be neighbours, so checking only consecutive days misses most pairs.
One pass with a dict, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It only counts days joined by a run of one-penny rises, so steady days with a dip between them are missed.
It moves the day to the wrong side and keys on `p + i`, which counts falls of a penny a day.
It counts each group of size `c` as `c - 1` pairs instead of `c * (c - 1) // 2`.
